task: External, citable literature anchors for the IOBRpy->Python+Rust port speedup campaign

internal_reference_point.metric: workflow_speedup (wall-clock, official-data workflow: sig scoring incl. ssGSEA, CIBERSORT perm=100, EPIC, quanTIseq, MCPcounter, ESTIMATE, count2tpm, annotation)
internal_reference_point.protocol: in-process perf_counter, median of 3 reps after 1 warmup, 224-core Linux, imvigor210_eset.parquet 872 genes x 348 samples
internal_reference_point.biggest_lever: CIBERSORT: 330 sklearn NuSVR(kernel='linear') fits (~0.2 s each on 531x22) dominate the original runtime

anchors.question: 1) IOBRpy preprint runtime/benchmark numbers (Python vs R)
anchors.finding: The IOBRpy preprint DOES report runtime numbers, but the only quantitative timing is a within-Python thread-scaling benchmark of CIBERSORT on a 936-sample cohort (OAKPOPLAR); the Python-vs-R comparison is qualitative per method, and the authors explicitly disclaim strict end-to-end comparability because Python timing included data loading while R timing started after loading.
verbatim_quotes: Runtime profiles differed by method rather than by programming language alone (Fig. 2a). In the 936-sample benchmark, mean CIBERSORT runtime decreased from 2,864.8 s with one Python thread to 368.4 s with eight threads and 209.7 s with 16 threads, yielding a 13.7-fold speed-up from one to 16 threads. Python was also faster for quanTIseq, ESTIMATE and EPIC in this benchmark, whereas R showed shorter recorded runtimes for MCP-counter and IPS.

The Python measurements included input-data loading, whereas R timing began after the data had been loaded; the apparent R advantage for some modules may therefore partly reflect the different timing scopes and should not be interpreted as a strict end-to-end comparison.

Runtime was recorded across 10 repeated runs for each setting; Python timing included input-data loading, whereas R timing began after the data had been loaded. CIBERSORT was additionally evaluated with 1, 8 and 16 Python threads.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: NOT a Python-vs-R speedup anchor (their fold number is threads-vs-threads inside Python). It IS the best external absolute-runtime anchor for the very software we ported: their CIBERSORT 2,864.8 s single-thread on 936 samples (~3.06 s/sample) vs our original-IOBRpy CIBERSORT ~66 s on 348 samples (~0.19 s/sample) shows how much signature-matrix size, perm count, cohort and timing scope move per-sample CIBERSORT cost across setups. Record as a literature anchor for 'CIBERSORT runtime magnitude in IOBRpy itself', with protocol mismatch flagged.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Different cohort (936-sample OP matrix vs our 348-sample IMvigor210 872-gene subset), unstated perm count in quoted text, Python timing scope includes input loading, thread counts 1/8/16 vs our measurement, different (unstated) hardware, 10 repeats vs our median-of-3.

anchors.question: 2a) Newman 2015 CIBERSORT paper runtime statements
anchors.finding: NO runtime/speed/timing statements in the abstract; only a qualitative scalability claim. (Verified via Europe PMC REST API.)
anchors.source: Newman et al. 2015, Nature Methods 12(5):453-457, PMID 25822800
verbatim_quotes: CIBERSORT should enable large-scale analysis of RNA mixtures for cellular biomarkers and therapeutic targets (http://cibersort.stanford.edu/).
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: None possible. Honest negative: the original CIBERSORT paper publishes no timing numbers to anchor against.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Abstract-level check only; full text behind publisher access, but no timing figures are known from the paper.

anchors.question: 2b) CIBERSORTx (Newman 2019 Nat Biotechnol) runtime statements
anchors.finding: NO runtime/minutes/timing statements in the abstract; only qualitative 'cost-effective, high-throughput' language. (Verified via Europe PMC REST API.)
anchors.source: Newman et al. 2019, Nature Biotechnology 37(7):773-782, PMID 31061481, PMC6610714
verbatim_quotes: We anticipate that digital cytometry will augment single-cell profiling efforts, enabling cost-effective, high-throughput tissue characterization without the need for antibodies, disaggregation or viable cells.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: None possible. Honest negative: no 'CIBERSORTx takes X minutes' statement exists in the paper abstract to cite.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Abstract verified; Methods sections of the paper and the cibersortx.stanford.edu web UI were not exhaustively searched for UI-level timing hints.

anchors.question: 2c) IOBR R papers (Frontiers 2021 / Cell Reports Methods 2024 / Med Research 2025) runtime statements
anchors.finding: No runtime/timing statements found in the IOBR R-package papers (Frontiers in Immunology 2021; IOBR2 Cell Reports Methods 2024; Med Research 2025). None of the three reports any benchmark seconds or speedup.
anchors.source: Zeng et al. 2021 Front. Immunol.; Zeng et al. 2024 Cell Rep Methods 4(12):100910; Fang et al. 2025 Med Research 1(1):136-140
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: None possible. Honest negative: the R-side papers publish no timing numbers, so no R-baseline anchor exists from the authors themselves.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Full texts of CRM 2024 and Med Research 2025 were not page-by-page scanned (paywalled); abstracts and long full-text excerpts examined contain no timings.

anchors.question: 2d) EXTERNAL measured CIBERSORT runtimes (third-party benchmark)
anchors.finding: Diaz-Mejia et al. benchmarked CIBERSORT (among 5 methods) on five scRNA-seq datasets on a 2-core laptop and published absolute computing times: CIBERSORT 'continuous' 75-9,330 s and 'binary' 46-1,522 s; slowest method tested; used the original LM22 signature (547 genes).

quoted_numbers.cpu: 3.1-GHz Intel Core i5, 2 cores, 16 GB RAM

verbatim_quotes: Computing times varied from 0.03s for METANEIGHBOR 'continuous', processing the 'PBMC-6-SeqWell' dataset, to 9,330s (2.6 hours) for CIBERSORT 'continuous', processing the 'PBMC-22-10X' dataset (Figure 6D and Supplementary Table 1).
Finally, the slowest methods were CIBERSORT 'binary' (46 to 1,522s) and CIBERSORT 'continuous' (75 to 9,330s).
All computing time measurements were made using a 3.1-GHz Intel Core i5 CPU with 2 cores and 16 GB RAM.
For example, for the analysis of the PBMC datasets with CIBERSORT 'continuous' we used the original LM22 signature with 547 genes.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Strongest external ABSOLUTE-runtime anchor for CIBERSORT's nu-SVR engine: independent authors measured hours-scale CIBERSORT runtimes, confirming the cost is real and known outside our machine. Maps as context for the size of the lever (CIBERSORT dominates), not as a ratio against our 97.13 s baseline.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Task is cell-cluster labeling on scRNA data (one mixture per cluster), not bulk TME deconvolution of 348 samples; 2-core 2015-era laptop vs our 224-core machine; perm count not stated in the quoted text; CIBERSORT run via its R source under their wrapper.

anchors.question: 3) gseapy paper: Rust rewrite speedup for enrichment scoring
anchors.finding: The gseapy paper (the tool IOBRpy itself uses for ssGSEA) reports an externally published Python->Rust rewrite speedup of the enrichment statistic: 3-fold (small library) to 80-fold (large library) single-threaded, still ~2-fold at 8 threads, memory 50 GB -> 1.4 GB in the large case.
verbatim_quotes: The Rust implementation of GSEApy is 3-fold faster than the Numpy version of GSEApy (v0.10.8) and uses >4-fold less memory.
For large gene set libraries (e.g. 2860 pathways in this article), it can run 80-fold faster without much more memory (Supplementary Fig. S1B).

we found that the Rust implementation was 3- to 80-fold faster in run time with one thread (Supplementary Fig. S1A). The run time with eight threads was decreased to a few minutes for both versions, but the Rust version was still 2-fold faster, and the memory cost was reduced from 50 GB to 1.4 GB (for the 2860 pathways).
While it took over 1 hour for GSEA-R to calculate the statistics for 2860 pathways, GSEA-P and GSEApy took 3.7 and 5.1 minutes, respectively.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Closest published PRECEDENT for exactly our move (Python scientific toolkit rewritten with a Rust core, bit-comparable statistic, speedup measured against the same package's prior pure-Python/Numpy version). Their 3-80x range brackets our current ~18x workflow speedup. Record as a literature anchor: 'peer-reviewed Python->Rust enrichment-scoring speedups of 3-80x are published'.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Baseline is gseapy's own earlier Numpy implementation, not IOBRpy; workload is the GSEA permutation statistic, not per-sample ssGSEA over an 872-gene x 348-sample matrix; their speedup depends strongly on gene-set-library size (3x small vs 80x large), so no single number transfers; hardware unstated in quotes.

anchors.question: 3b) gseapy ssGSEA-specific runtime benchmark
anchors.finding: NO ssGSEA-specific runtime benchmark found in the gseapy paper or repo; all published timing claims concern the GSEA/prerank permutation statistic. The ssGSEA module shares the Rust core (ssgsea_rs), but no ssGSEA timing table exists.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: None directly. Honest negative: for the ssGSEA stage of our workflow specifically, no published external timing exists; nearest neighbor is A6.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Repo issues were not exhaustively read for user-reported timings; claim covers paper + README + docs as of 2026-09-07.

anchors.question: 4a) sklearn NuSVR linear-kernel slowness: near-identical case report
anchors.finding: A public scikit-learn issue reports NuSVR(kernel='linear') on a 547x22 matrix (essentially the LM22 CIBERSORT problem shape; our fits are 531x22) running >3 hours without returning, and R (e1071/libsvm) being faster on the same problem. Issue closed with no fix; discussion attributes it to convergence/scaling behavior of libsvm's nu-SVR.
anchors.source: scikit-learn GitHub issue #11079, opened 2018-05-09 by PhungVanDuy (sklearn 0.19.1)
verbatim_quotes: I performed the NuSVR (linear kernel) function with matrix input has to shape is 547 x 22 and output 574. But it running too slow! I tried it with R, however, R run faster!
I run it more than 3 hours but still have no results. I think has an error here!
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Anchor for the MECHANISM claim: sklearn NuSVR(linear) on exactly the CIBERSORT problem shape is publicly documented as pathologically slow (7 years before our port). Supports 'the 330 NuSVR fits dominating our original 97.13 s is a known, externally reported bottleneck'. NOT a quantitative anchor (no controlled timing).
anchors.protocol_caveats: Anecdotal single-user report; features possibly unscaled; 2018 sklearn version; no maintainer resolution on record; pathological tail behavior of libsvm nu-SVR convergence depends on data, so '>3 h' cannot be compared with our ~0.2 s/fit typical case.

anchors.question: 4b) sklearn official docs: libsvm-based SVC/SVR complexity vs liblinear
anchors.finding: scikit-learn's official SVM user guide states the libsvm-based implementation scales between O(n_features x n_samples^2) and O(n_features x n_samples^3), and that the liblinear-based LinearSVC/LinearSVR are 'much more efficient' / 'a faster implementation' for the linear case. NuSVR has no liblinear counterpart in sklearn (this is why the bottleneck has no drop-in sklearn fix and motivates the Rust core).
anchors.source: scikit-learn user guide, section 1.4 (SVM), 'Complexity' and implementation notes (fetched 2026-09-07, sklearn 1.9.0 docs)
verbatim_quotes: The QP solver used by the libsvm-based implementation scales between O(n_features x n_samples^2) and O(n_features x n_samples^3) depending on how efficiently the libsvm cache is used in practice (dataset dependent).

For the linear case, the algorithm used in LinearSVC by the liblinear implementation is much more efficient than its libsvm-based SVC counterpart and can scale almost linearly to millions of samples and/or features.

There are three different implementations of Support Vector Regression: SVR, NuSVR and LinearSVR. LinearSVR provides a faster implementation than SVR but only considers the linear kernel, while NuSVR implements a slightly different formulation than SVR and LinearSVR.
Internally, we use libsvm [12] and liblinear [11] to handle all computations.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Authoritative anchor for the complexity argument behind our CIBERSORT lever. Supports the theory 'libsvm nu-SVR is the quadratic-cost component'; supplies no numbers of its own.
anchors.protocol_caveats: Documentation statement, not a measurement; complexity bounds describe scaling, not wall-clock on 531x22.

anchors.question: 4c) Published benchmark of a libsvm alternative: ThunderSVM (and the SVR row)
anchors.finding: Peer-reviewed JMLR paper: ThunderSVM (GPU + multi-core CPU reimplementation of LibSVM incl. nu-SVR, producing 'identical SVMs') is 'generally an order of magnitude faster than LibSVM' - over 100x with GPUs, over 10x on CPUs. Their SVR benchmark (e2006-tfidf, 16,087 samples, RBF kernel): LibSVM 9,161 s vs ThunderSVM 691 s (CPU, 13.3x) / 343.5 s (GPU, 26.7x).
anchors.source: Wen, Shi, Li, He, Chen 2018, JMLR 19:797-801
verbatim_quotes: Our experimental results show that ThunderSVM is generally an order of magnitude faster than LibSVM while producing identical SVMs.
ThunderSVM when using GPUs is over 100 times faster than LibSVM. When running on CPUs, it is over 10 times faster than LibSVM.
ThunderSVM consistently outperforms LibSVM without OpenMP by one to two orders of magnitude, LibSVM with OpenMP by 10x times.
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Peer-reviewed quantitative anchor that re-implementing the same libsvm solver natively/parallel yields 10-100x with identical outputs - the same claim class as our bit-exact Rust NuSVR replacing sklearn's libsvm wrapper. Their 'identical SVMs' claim parallels our bit-exactness. Numbers do NOT transfer (RBF kernel, 16k-sample dataset, GPU).
anchors.protocol_caveats: Gaussian kernel (not linear); 16,087-sample financial dataset (not 531x22); Tesla P100 GPU / 2x Xeon E5-2640 v4 workstation; parallelized algorithm (our comparison is single-fit serial vs serial, plus batching); speedup is over LibSVM C, not over sklearn's Cython wrapper overhead.

anchors.finding: Latest release is 0.2.1 (wheel uploaded 2026-08-17T17:43:39Z), so 0.2.0 is NOT the latest. 0.2.0 wheel was uploaded 2026-07-12T11:56:59Z (July, not August). No changelog text is published.
anchors.source: PyPI JSON API for package iobrpy (queried 2026-09-07)
verbatim_quotes: upload_time_iso_8601: 2026-08-17T17:43:39Z (iobrpy-0.2.1 manylinux wheel)
upload_time_iso_8601: 2026-07-12T11:56:59Z (iobrpy-0.2.0 manylinux_2_38 wheel)
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: No timing content. Pins the moving target: our bit-exact baseline (upstream IOBRpy at commit e3808db / v0.2.0) is one release behind PyPI latest 0.2.1 as of 2026-09-07 - worth noting in any writeup of the port, and a check-item that 0.2.1 did not itself add a Rust/native accelerator (README/PyPI description shows no such claim).

anchors.question: 6) Prior Rust/WASM ports of CIBERSORT or libsvm-based deconvolution
anchors.finding: crates.io has ZERO crates matching 'cibersort' (API: total 0) - no published Rust CIBERSORT crate exists. However, adjacent prior/parallel work exists on GitHub: (a) LCGaoZzz/python-cibersort-rs - 'Python CIBERSORT v1.04 implementation with a bundled Rust accelerator' (PyO3/Rayon nu-SVR, R-compatible Mersenne-Twister, rust/libsvm/numpy engines, bundled benchmarks); (b) ricardofrantz/libsvm-rs (crates.io libsvm-rs, created 2026-02-09, 335 downloads) - pure-Rust LIBSVM reimplementation covering all 5 SVM types incl. nu-SVR, wasm32 compile-checked; (c) sinmojito/quantiseq-rust (crates.io) - pure-Rust quanTIseq deconvolution port, numeric parity vs Bioconductor quantiseqr. No WASM CIBERSORT port found.
verbatim_quotes: An installable Python implementation of the CIBERSORT v1.04 deconvolution pipeline with a bundled Rust accelerator. It runs without R and exposes both a Python API and a command-line interface. (python-cibersort-rs README)
Pure Rust reimplementation of LIBSVM - zero FFI, drop-in model & CLI compatibility, differential parity tests vs upstream C++, optional serde/rayon/wasm (libsvm-rs README)
All 5 SVM types: C-SVC, nu-SVC, one-class SVM, epsilon-SVR, nu-SVR (-s 0..4) (libsvm-rs README)
Pure-Rust port of quanTIseq (Finotello et al. 2019) immune-cell deconvolution ... validated for numeric parity against the Bioconductor quantiseqr package. (quantiseq-rust)
anchors.mapping_to_workflow_speedup: Novelty check, not a numeric anchor: no published Rust CIBERSORT crate on crates.io (our cibersort_core is not anticipated on crates.io), but a GitHub Python+Rust CIBERSORT accelerator exists, a pure-Rust LIBSVM (incl. nu-SVR) exists, and a Rust quanTIseq with parity validation exists. Cite these as related work; do NOT claim first-ever Rust CIBERSORT without qualifying against python-cibersort-rs.
anchors.protocol_caveats: crates.io search is exact-string; GitHub repos were not cloned/benchmarked, their README claims (including parity and benchmark claims) are unverified; python-cibersort-rs authorship/date relative to this campaign not established.

negative_findings_summary: IOBRpy preprint: NO Python-vs-R wall-clock speedup number exists - only in-Python CIBERSORT thread scaling (13.7x, 1->16 threads) plus qualitative per-method direction, with an explicit authors' caveat that the timing scopes differ.
Newman 2015 (CIBERSORT) and Newman 2019 (CIBERSORTx): no runtime statements in abstracts - no 'takes X minutes' claim to cite.
IOBR R papers (2021/2024/2025): no runtime or benchmark numbers found.
gseapy: no ssGSEA-specific runtime benchmark published (claims cover the GSEA permutation statistic).
No crate named cibersort exists on crates.io; no WASM CIBERSORT port found.

No published controlled benchmark comparing sklearn NuSVR(linear) head-to-head against liblinear/thunderSVM on CIBERSORT-shaped (531-547 x 22) problems exists - only the anecdotal issue #11079, official complexity statements, and ThunderSVM's RBF-kernel benchmarks.

recommended_primary_anchor.for_python_to_rust_speedup_claim: A6 (gseapy, Bioinformatics 2023, 3-80x Rust-vs-Numpy for the same package's enrichment statistic) - peer-reviewed, same claim class, brackets our ~18x
recommended_primary_anchor.for_cibersort_bottleneck_claim: A5 (F1000Research 2019, CIBERSORT 75-9,330 s on 2-core i5) + A8 (sklearn #11079, NuSVR linear on 547x22 >3 h) + A9 (sklearn docs complexity) + A10 (ThunderSVM 10-100x, identical SVMs)
recommended_primary_anchor.for_runtime_magnitude_in_iobrpy_itself: A1 (IOBRpy preprint, CIBERSORT 2,864.8 s single-thread on 936 samples, 13.7x thread scaling)
recommended_primary_anchor.record_protocol_note: Every anchor differs from our protocol (in-process perf_counter, median of 3 after 1 warmup, 224 cores, IMvigor210 872x348); none can be subtracted from or divided into our 97.13 s -> 5.4 s measurement; they are magnitude/context anchors only.
